title: Playing Closed & Locked Positions
blurb: When the center locks and the tactics go quiet, the game is not over — it is just beginning. Learn the eight disciplines that turn a 'nothing' position into a win.

principle.markdown:
When the center locks, it is easy to feel there is nothing to do but shuffle pieces and hope the opponent slips. That feeling is a lie the position tells you. **A closed position is not the absence of a plan — it is a plan you have not named yet.**

Whenever you are stuck, run down the four things a closed position *always* offers:

1. **Maneuver** — reroute your worst-placed piece to its best square (the knight tour Nd2–f1–g3 is the archetype). Nothing is symmetric once one knight reaches a great square and the other is still bad.
2. **Restrict** — take space and squares away from the opponent until their pieces have no active move. Every square you deny is counterplay you never have to meet.
3. **Second weakness** — one weakness a defender can guard; two, on opposite wings, stretches the defense past breaking. Closed positions are where you *manufacture* the second target.
4. **Time the break** — the locked structure has a lever (a pawn break) that opens the position on *your* terms. You prepare it fully, then play it — you do not lash out with it early.

"Stall and pray" is not a fifth option that appears when the first four run out. The first four never run out. If all you can find is a waiting move, you have stopped *choosing* a plan, not run out of them.
principle.remember: A locked position is a plan you haven't named yet — maneuver, restrict, make a second weakness, or time the break.

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O Be7 6. Re1 b5 7. Bb3 d6 8. c3 O-O 9. h3 Na5 10. Bc2 c5 11. d4 Qc7 12. Nbd2 Nc6 13. d5 Nd8 14. a4 Rb8 15. axb5 axb5 16. b4 *
illustrations.source: Karpov–Unzicker, Nice Olympiad 1974. Move-score is public fact; all commentary here is original (clean-room, spec 227).

focus.text: Ten moves in and nothing is resolved: both sides are developed, the center pawns face off, the position looks nearly symmetric. This is exactly the moment a stronger player does NOT drift. The structure is about to tell White what the plan is.

Black has just rerouted the knight back to c6, keeping the tension. White must now decide the character of the whole game. A neutral developing move leaves the center fluid and White reacting to Black. There is a move that seizes space and hands White a concrete, multi-move plan.

ask.prompt: White to move. Don't keep the center fluid — commit to a structure that gives you a plan. What do you play?
ask.explain: Capturing (dxc5 or dxe5) or a neutral move like Nf1 first keeps the center fluid and hands Black the freeing ...d5 break — you stay reactive. 13.d5 is the plan-defining move: it locks the center, gains space, and immediately tells both sides where to play (White on the queenside, Black on the kingside). The mistake is treating a quiet position as one where any move will do — here the wrong choice surrenders the initiative for the whole middlegame.

focus.text: 13.d5 locks the center. Now the position is no longer symmetric or vague — it has a grain. White's pawn chain points at the queenside (c3-d5 → the c/b-files), so that is where White plays. Black's points kingside. The plan is no longer a mystery; it was hiding in the pawn structure.

14.a4, 15.axb5 and 16.b4 execute the plan the structure named: open the a-file, fix Black's b5/c5 pawns as targets, and clamp the queenside. This is not shuffling — it is restriction and a second front, played move by move. Karpov will pile up on the a-file next; Black has no matching activity. THIS is what a closed position's plan looks like when you name it instead of stalling.

questions.prompt: The center is about to lock and you catch yourself thinking 'I can only find moves that stall.' What has actually happened?
options: The position is objectively equal, so there really is nothing to do but wait.
You have stopped naming a concrete plan — the position still offers maneuver, restriction, a second weakness, and a timed break.
You need to force a pawn break immediately to create something out of nothing.
questions.explain: 'Nothing to do' is a feeling, not a fact about the position. The mistake in option 1 is mistaking your own failure to choose a plan for the position being empty. Option 3 is the opposite mistake — lashing out with an unprepared break that just makes weaknesses. A closed position always offers the four plans; being stuck means you stopped picking one.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four real plans a closed position offers?
options: Maneuver your worst-placed piece to its best square.
Restrict the opponent until their pieces have no active move.
Shuffle a rook back and forth and wait for the opponent to blunder.
Create a second weakness on the other wing to stretch the defense.
questions.explain: Options 1, 2 and 4 are three of the four standard plans (the fourth is timing the pawn break). Option 3 is the exact anti-plan this lesson kills: 'shuffle and pray' is not a fifth option that appears when the others run out — the others never run out. Waiting is only a plan when it is real prophylaxis or zugzwang play, not aimless shuffling.

questions.prompt: The center is locked and White has just traded on b5. Play the move that clamps the queenside and turns Black's b5/c5 pawns into fixed targets.
questions.explain: A passive move like Ra2 or Nf1 here lets Black relieve the pressure with ...c4 or activate with ...Nb7-c5, and White's space edge dissolves into more shuffling. 16.b4 fixes b5 and c5 as permanent targets and clamps the queenside, and the half-open a-file gives White a concrete file to pile up on. That is restriction plus a second front — a plan, not a wait.

questions.prompt: The center just locked with d5. In your own words, name a concrete plan for White here and say what makes it a plan rather than shuffling.
questions.modelAnswer: The locked pawn chain (c3–d5) points at the queenside, so White plays there: expand with a4 and b4 to open the a-file and fix Black's b5/c5 pawns as targets, then double rooks on the a-file — a first weakness plus, potentially, a second front. Meanwhile reroute the worst piece, the d2-knight, via f1 to g3 or e3 toward a strong square, and keep Black's ...f5 counter-break restrained. The common mistake is treating the quiet as emptiness: either drifting with aimless rook moves (no target, no route) or lashing out with an unprepared break that only creates weaknesses. A plan names a target AND a route and improves your position move by move; shuffling does neither.
rubric: Names a concrete target or file (the queenside / a-file / Black's b5-c5 pawns), not just 'improve the position'.
Includes a piece route or pawn break (a4/b4, or the Nd2-f1-g3 maneuver), not only defense.
Distinguishes purposeful maneuvering from aimless shuffling — a plan has a target and a route.
Does not advocate an unprepared pawn break that just creates weaknesses.

modules.title: The plan comes from the pawn structure

principle.markdown:
In an open position pieces choose the plan. In a **locked** one the **pawns choose it for you** — and they say it out loud if you listen. Two rules cover almost everything:

**1. Play where your chain points.** A pawn chain is an arrow. The pawns that ram forward (say a White c3–d4 duo, or an e5 spearhead) claim space on that flank, and behind that space your pieces have room to gather and attack. The other player owns the *opposite* flank for the same reason. So do not fight for the square where the enemy pawns give *him* the space — expand where *your* pawns give *you* the space, and make him defend on your terms.

**2. Attack the base of the chain.** A pawn chain is only as solid as the pawn at its back. The head (the most advanced pawn) is defended by the pawn behind it; the **base** is defended by nothing but pieces. Lever it with a pawn break — a French player meets White's d4–e5 chain with **...c5**, hammering the base d4, not the head e5. Crack the base and the whole chain sags.

Put together: the structure names your flank *and* your target. When you feel planless in a closed game, you have usually just stopped reading the pawns.
principle.remember: Your pawn chain is a compass and a target list: play on the side it points, and pry at the pawn it stands on.

1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Bb4 4. e3 d5 5. a3 Bxc3+ 6. bxc3 c5 7. cxd5 exd5
8. Bd3 O-O 9. Ne2 b6 10. O-O Ba6 11. Bxa6 Nxa6 12. Bb2 Qd7 13. a4 Rfe8
14. Qd3 c4 15. Qc2 Nb8 16. Rae1 Nc6 17. Ng3 Na5 18. f3 Nb3 19. e4 Qxa4
20. e5 Nd7 21. Qf2 g6 22. f4 f5 23. exf6 Nxf6 24. f5 *
illustrations.source: Botvinnik vs. Capablanca, AVRO 1938 (Nimzo-Indian, E40); move-score is public fact. Annotations original, clean-room (spec 227). Shown through 24.f5.

focus.text: After 6.bxc3 the structure is set for the whole game. White accepts doubled c-pawns to build a broad centre (c3–d4 plus e3), and gets a central/kingside pawn majority; Black gets the queenside majority (a-, b-, c-pawns). Neither side chose a plan yet — the pawns just chose it for both of them.

The picture is now clear. White's pawns point at the centre and kingside (d4–e3, later e4–f4–f5); Black's point at the queenside. Each side should expand where its own pawns give space — and that split, not any single move, is the plan.

14...c4! Black commits to his flank: he locks the queenside, fixes his 3-vs-2 majority, and frees the c6-square route ...Nc6-a5-b3 to plant a knight in White's camp. But locking the queenside also **releases the tension on d4** — it tells White the centre is his to open at leisure. Reading the structure, White now knows exactly where to play.

18...Nb3 looks menacing — a knight deep in White's position — but it "bites on granite": it attacks nothing that matters and cannot be supported by more pieces quickly. Meanwhile White has quietly finished preparing with f3.

ask.prompt: White to move. Black is massing on the queenside where HE is strong. Stop admiring his knight and play the move the pawn structure has been asking for since move 7.
ask.explain: Fussing over the b3-knight (e.g. a passive queenside shuffle) plays on Black's side of the board, where his majority dominates — exactly the wrong flank. 19.e4! opens the centre and kingside, the side WHITE's pawns point at, converting the structural majority into an attack. The b3-knight is a spectator; the game is decided where the pawns aim.

focus.text: 20.e5 — the chain advances and gains space, its head now pointing straight at the black king. This is the structure paying off: the e5-spearhead is the launch pad for the f4–f5 break to come.

24.f5! The break lands. Every White move since move 7 flowed from one reading of the structure — my majority is central/kingside, so that is where I open lines and attack. Black's queenside play (the proud b3-knight, ...Qxa4) never touched the real battlefield.

questions.prompt: White has the c3–d4 pawn mass (and e3 in reserve); Black has a queenside pawn majority. Which flank should White plan to play on, and why?
options: The queenside, to attack and win the doubled c-pawns before Black's majority rolls.
The centre and kingside, where the c3–d4–e3 pawns give space and back an e3–e4 advance.
Neither flank; the doubled pawns are a long-term weakness, so trade down toward a draw.
questions.explain: Playing on the queenside walks straight into Black's strength — that is where HIS majority lives, and ...c4/...b5 come with tempo. The c3-pawns are not a target you can attack, they are a wall that supports d4. White's trump is the central/kingside space, so the plan is e3–e4–e5 and an f-pawn advance where his pawns point. Treating a dynamic structure as merely "bad" (option 3) and steering for a draw throws away the exact asset the pawns handed him.

questions.prompt: Black has just planted ...Nb3 and clamped the queenside with ...c4. White has prepared with f3. Play the move the structure demands.
questions.explain: A queenside reply (say a5, or spending moves to evict the knight) fights on Black's flank, where his majority rules — the wrong side of the board. 19.e4! strikes in the centre/kingside, the direction White's pawns point, and opens the position for his pieces and the coming f4–f5. The b3-knight bites on granite: leave it and play where you are strong.

questions.prompt: French Advance: White's pawn chain runs d4–e5, its head pointing at your kingside. As Black, strike at the RIGHT link of the chain.
questions.explain: Do not attack the head e5 first (an early ...f6 pries the head but opens your own king before you are ready); the base of the chain is d4, and it is defended only by pieces. 3...c5! hammers that base — if White ever loses d4 the whole e5-chain collapses. Attack the base, not the head.

questions.prompt: In your own words: state White's plan AND Black's plan from this structure, and say what makes each a plan drawn from the pawns rather than a random move.
questions.modelAnswer: The pawns split the board. White's majority and space are central/kingside (d4, e3, then e3–e4–e5 and f4–f5), so White plans to expand and attack THERE, where his pawns point. Black's majority is queenside (a-, b-, c-pawns), so Black plans ...c4, ...b5 and piece play on that wing, plus pressure on White's fixed c3/d4 pawns. Each is a real plan because the structure names both the flank and the lever in advance; the recurring mistake is playing on the enemy's flank — White grubbing after the c-pawns on the queenside, or Black trying to defend the kingside squares White's pawns already own — which spends moves where you are structurally weak instead of where you are strong.
rubric: Assigns White the centre/kingside and Black the queenside, and ties each to that side's pawn majority/space.
Names a concrete lever or break for at least one side (e.g. White e3–e4–e5/f4–f5; Black ...c4/...b5).
Explains WHY it counts as a plan: the pawns fix the flank and the target ahead of time.
Flags the mistake of playing on the opponent's strong flank instead of your own.

modules.title: Improve your worst piece; maneuver to the best square

principle.markdown:
When the pawns lock, tactics go quiet and **piece quality** decides the game. The move you are hunting for is almost never a lunge — it is a **regroup**. Find your worst-placed piece and give it a route to the best square it can reach.

Two rules of thumb do most of the work. First, in a blocked centre a **knight is usually worth more than a bishop**: fixed pawns are walls a bishop cannot see past, but a knight hops over them and lands on an **outpost** — a square no enemy pawn can ever challenge, because the pawns that would attack it are gone or frozen. Second, improvement is **slow and often backward-looking**: the classic knight route Nf3–e1–d3 *retreats* before it advances, and that is correct — the knight did nothing on f3 and will do everything from d3.

So the plan in a locked position is rarely one move; it is a **maneuver**. Ask "which of my pieces is worst, and where does it belong?", then spend three or four quiet moves getting it there. Only once your pieces sit on their best squares do you time the pawn break — improving the worst piece first is exactly what makes the eventual break work.
principle.remember: In a locked position, find your worst piece and reroute it to its best square — the slow regroup beats the lunge, and a knight on an outpost outweighs a hemmed-in bishop.

1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6 5. Nf3 O-O 6. Be2 e5 7. O-O Nc6 8. d5 Ne7 9. Ne1 Nd7 10. Nd3 f5 *
illustrations.source: Standard opening theory (King's Indian Defence, Classical Main Line / Mar del Plata, ECO E97). The move-score is public opening theory; all annotations are original (clean-room, spec 227).

focus.text: 8.d5 locks the centre: the e4/d5 vs d6/e5 chain is fixed and will not dissolve. From here there are no tactics to find — the game becomes a maneuvering contest, and whoever gets their pieces to better squares first will get to dictate the coming pawn break.

Black shows the idea in miniature: the c6-knight had no future against the d5 pawn, so ...Ne7 reroutes it toward g6 (and frees the f-pawn for ...f5). Now it is White's turn to find White's own worst piece and give it a home.

ask.prompt: White to move, centre locked. The f3-knight is doing nothing behind the fixed chain. Begin the regroup — where should it head?
ask.explain: Behind the locked e4/d5 chain the f3-knight has no active square and merely blocks the f-pawn — leaving it there (or lashing out with a premature f4/Bg5) wastes the position's logic. Ne1 is the model reroute: the knight heads e1–d3, where it supports the thematic c5 break and covers b4, e5 and f4. Nd2 (aiming …Nf1–e3 or supporting a later f-push) is the other reroute and is accepted. The mistake is any plan that leaves your worst piece passive while you play on the wings.

focus.text: 9.Ne1 looks like a step backward — and it is, deliberately. This is the slow regroup: a knight that retreats to reach a better square is improving, not retreating. The route is Ne1–d3.

10.Nd3 completes the maneuver. Compare the knight now to three moves ago: from d3 it braces the c5 break, eyes b4 and f4, and reinforces e5 — the worst piece has become one of the best. Only now is White ready to fight for the break.

10...f5 — Black has finished the mirror-image regroup (…Ne7 and …Nd7 clearing the way) and strikes. Both sides improved their worst pieces first; the pawn levers come only after the pieces are home. That ordering — regroup, then break — is the whole lesson.

questions.prompt: The centre is locked (e4/d5 vs d6/e5). Which is White's worst-placed piece, and what is the plan?
options: The e2-bishop — trade it off at once with Bg4 to simplify.
The f3-knight — blocked by the fixed centre; reroute it Ne1–d3 to support the c5 break.
Nothing is misplaced; just push the h-pawn and hope for a kingside attack.
questions.explain: The f3-knight is the worst piece: behind the fixed e4/d5 chain it has no forward square and only blocks the f-pawn, so Ne1–d3 reroutes it to where it braces c5 and covers b4/e5/f4. Grabbing at Bg4 trades a perfectly good bishop for nothing, and shoving the h-pawn creates weaknesses on the side where you have no play — both are the classic error of acting on the wings before you have fixed your worst-placed piece.

questions.prompt: In a fully blocked pawn centre, which minor piece is usually stronger, and why?
options: The bishop — its long diagonals always dominate.
The knight — it hops over the fixed pawns onto outposts the enemy pawns can never challenge, while a bishop is walled in by its own locked chain.
They are always equal; piece value never depends on the pawn structure.
questions.explain: With the centre locked, knights ≥ bishops: the fixed pawns are walls a bishop cannot see past, but a knight jumps them to sit on an outpost. The mistake is treating piece values as fixed and, worse, trading your knight for a bishop (or keeping a bishop buried behind its own pawn chain) in precisely the structure where the knight is the better minor piece.

questions.prompt: White to move. The e3-knight is the worst piece behind the locked centre — send it to its permanent home. Play the move.
questions.explain: Nd5 plants the knight on the one hole nothing can ever challenge — no black pawn can reach c6 or e6 to hit it — and from d5 it strikes c7, e7, f6 and b6 while the backward d6-pawn stays weak. The tempting Nf5? simply drops the knight to ...gxf5, and leaving it on e3 — a passive square whose only real forward outpost is the very d5 hole the knight should be occupying — wastes the whole idea: improve your worst piece onto its best square, not a square your own pawns duplicate.

questions.prompt: White to move, centre locked. In your own words: name White's worst-placed piece, give it a concrete route to a better square, and say what the impatient alternative would be and why it is worse.
questions.modelAnswer: White's worst piece is the f3-knight: the fixed e4/d5 vs d6/e5 chain leaves it no active square and it blocks the f-pawn. The model route is Nf3–e1–d3 — Ne1 first, then Nd3 — where the knight supports the thematic c5 break and covers b4, e5 and f4, turning the worst piece into one of the best. Black answers with the mirror regroup (…Nd7 and …Ne7–g6, freeing …f5). The impatient alternative — lunging with an immediate f4 or c5, or trading off a healthy piece, before the knight is rerouted — is the mistake: it opens lines while your worst piece is still passive and hands the opponent the more harmonious position. First improve the worst piece; then time the break.
rubric: Identifies the f3-knight (not the e2-bishop) as the worst piece, and says why — the locked centre leaves it no square.
Gives a concrete route to a real square: Ne1–d3 (a Nd2 reroute is acceptable), not merely 'improve it'.
Names what the improved knight achieves: supports the c5 break, covers b4/e5/f4.
Flags the impatient error: a premature break (f4 or c5) or a needless trade before the regroup is finished.

principle.markdown:
You have a plan. So does the opponent. In an open game your own initiative can outrun his; in a **closed** one it usually can't — nothing is forcing, so his plan gets time to arrive. **Prophylaxis** is the discipline of spending a move on *his* idea before you spend the next on yours: find the break or maneuver he is preparing, and quietly take it away first.

The method is one question, asked every move: **"If it were his turn, what would he want to play?"** Name that move. If it would genuinely improve his position — a freeing pawn break, a knight reaching a great square, a rook swinging to the open file — deny it *now*, while it is still cheap. A break you prevent costs him nothing to lose and you nothing to hold; a break you allow can take ten moves to repair.

This is why Petrosian and Kramnik look, at a glance, like they are doing *nothing*. They are removing the opponent's chances one by one. Petrosian would reroute a knight for three moves purely to cover the square a break needs; Kramnik met Kasparov's ferocious initiative with the Berlin, trading the queens off before an attack could exist — neutralize first, create later.

Prophylaxis is not passivity and it is not fear. It is initiative aimed at the opponent's plan instead of your own: you still intend to win, but you make his position worse before you make yours better. In a locked position, the player who is never surprised is usually the player who wins.
principle.remember: Before you improve your own position, ask what the opponent wants — and take that away first.

[Result "*"]

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 Nf6 4. O-O Nxe4 5. d4 Nd6 6. Bxc6 dxc6 7. dxe5 Nf5 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8 *
illustrations.source: Berlin Defence, Ruy Lopez (opening theory; the line Kramnik used to blunt Kasparov, World Championship, London 2000). Move-score is public theory; annotations original (clean-room, spec 227).

focus.text: 3...Nf6 — the Berlin. Against an attacker of Kasparov's power, Kramnik does not try to out-punch him; he steers toward a structure where an attack has nothing to hit. Choosing the battlefield IS prophylaxis.
5...Nd6 — Black hands the knight back and invites simplification. He is not grabbing material; he is trading dynamism for a position White cannot set fire to.
6.Bxc6 — and Black must choose a recapture. This is the prophylactic fork in the road.

ask.prompt: Black to recapture on c6. The whole plan is to reach a queenless, attack-proof endgame. Which recapture serves that plan?
ask.explain: 6...bxc6 keeps a healthier pawn majority but leaves the queens on and the d-file closed — exactly the messy, dynamic middlegame Kasparov wants. 6...dxc6 opens the d-file on purpose so the queens come off next move (8.Qxd8+). You accept doubled c-pawns as the price of neutralizing the attack before it can start — prevent his plan, then worry about your own.

focus.text: 8.Qxd8+ — the queens leave the board. With no queens, the attacking chances Kasparov lives on simply do not exist; Black's slightly worse structure is a problem for move 40, not move 12.

8...Kxd8 — Black even gives up castling, and it doesn't matter: in a queenless, half-open position the king is a fighting piece, not a target. The attack was prevented before it was ever launched. That is prophylaxis at the level of a whole game plan.

1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O Be7 6. Re1 b5 7. Bb3 d6 8. c3 O-O 9. h3 Na5 10. Bc2 c5 11. d4 Qc7 12. Nbd2 Nc6 13. d5 Nd8 14. Nf1 Ne8 15. Ne3 g6 16. g4 *
illustrations.source: Closed Ruy Lopez, Chigorin System (standard opening theory). Move-score is public theory; annotations original (clean-room, spec 227).

focus.text: 13.d5 — White locks the centre (pawns e4/d5 against e5/d6). Now nothing is forcing and the game will be decided by plans, not blows. Black's one source of counterplay in this structure is the ...f5 break; almost everything else is frozen.

14.Nf1 — a move that attacks nothing and looks like a loss of time. It is pure prophylaxis: the knight is heading to e3, the square from which it will smother Black's ...f5 plan before White commits to anything of his own.

15.Ne3 — there it is. The knight now guards f5 and eyes d5; if Black plays ...f5 anyway, gxf5 or exf5 leaves e4/e6 holes and Black's break has only opened lines for White. The opponent's plan is neutralized. Only now, with ...f5 defanged, does White expand with g4 and his own kingside play — his plan comes second, on purpose.
16.g4 — the initiative at last, and it is safe. This is the whole lesson in one game: White spent moves 14–15 removing Black's counterplay, and move 16 pursuing his own. Neutralize, then create.

questions.prompt: The centre is locked and it is your move. What is the prophylactic question to ask FIRST?
options: Where is my fastest attack, so I can start it immediately?
What does my opponent want to play next — and can I prevent it cheaply now?
Which piece can I trade to simplify toward a draw?
questions.explain: Rushing your own attack (option 1) is the classic closed-position error: nothing is forcing, so his counterplay arrives while you are still setting up. Trading toward a draw (option 3) abandons a position you can play to win. Prophylaxis asks his plan first — here Black's only break is ...f5, so you deny f5 (Ne3) before expanding. Prevent, then create.

questions.prompt: Black's only counterplay in this locked centre is the ...f5 break. Play the prophylactic move that takes it away.
questions.explain: Ne3 completes the Nd2–f1–e3 regroup: the knight guards f5 and d5, so ...f5 now just opens lines into Black's own camp. Charging in with g4 first would be your plan before his is stopped — Black answers ...f5 and gets exactly the counterplay you were supposed to prevent. Neutralize the break, THEN push g4.

questions.prompt: In your own words: what is Black's plan in this locked position, and what is White's prophylactic response before starting his own play?
questions.modelAnswer: Black's plan is the ...f5 pawn break — the only way to generate counterplay in this frozen centre (prepare it with ...g6, ...Ng7 or ...Nf6, ...f5). White's prophylaxis is the knight route Nf1–e3: from e3 the knight covers f5 (and d5), so ...f5 no longer frees Black — it just opens lines White is better placed to use. The mistake to avoid is launching White's own kingside expansion (g4, Ng3, Kg2, Rg1) BEFORE ...f5 is stopped: play your plan first and Black gets in ...f5 with real counterplay, turning a comfortable edge into a double-edged race. Prevent his break, then pursue your attack.
rubric: Identifies ...f5 as Black's counterplay / break in this structure.
Names a concrete prophylactic route or square (Nf1–e3 / a knight covering f5), not just 'defend'.
States the order: neutralize the opponent's break BEFORE starting White's own expansion.
Warns against rushing White's own plan (g4 etc.) while ...f5 is still available.

questions.prompt: Kramnik chose the Berlin to meet Kasparov's attacking power. Which statement best captures the prophylactic idea behind it?
options: It sets a sharp trap that wins material by force in the opening.
It heads for a queenless structure so the attack Kasparov relies on can never form — neutralize first, play for the win later.
It is a purely passive, drawish choice that gives up on winning entirely.
questions.explain: The Berlin is not a trap (option 1) and not surrender (option 3) — treating prophylaxis as 'playing for a draw' misreads it. Trading the queens off removes the opponent's *strongest weapon* before it can be used; Black then plays the resulting endgame for a full result. Prophylaxis is initiative aimed at the opponent's plan, not the absence of ambition.

principle.markdown:
A single weakness is rarely enough to win. Give the defender **one** target and, in a closed or balanced position, they can usually plant a piece in front of it and hold forever — no matter how many attackers you stack up, the defender only needs enough guards for that one square. Attackers pile on; nothing breaks.

The win comes from a **second** weakness, far from the first. Step one: **fix** the first target so the enemy pieces stay chained to it. Step two: **open a new front** on the other wing. Now the same limited defensive force has to cover two distant points at once — and pieces cannot be in two places. Shuttle the pressure between the fronts, and sooner or later the stretched defense drops something.

Karpov's boa-constrictor squeeze is the model. In **Karpov–Unzicker, Nice 1974**, he fixed Black's queenside with a4 and b4, tied every Black piece to defending it, and only *then* switched the play to the other wing, where the overstretched defense finally cracked. Capablanca did the same in his endgames: one weakness to bind, a second to break. The order is the lesson — you do not win by attacking the weakness harder, you win by making a second one.
principle.remember: One weakness a defender can hold forever — fix it, then create a SECOND on the far wing and stretch the defense until it snaps.

focus.text: Both sides are fully developed and the centre is about to lock. There is no open file and no attack — exactly the moment where a player wrongly feels they can 'only shuffle.' Nothing will be decided in the centre, so the game moves to the wings.

ask.prompt: White to move. The centre is locked and Black has no active plan. Start the bind — which pawn move creates the first fixed target, on the wing where White has space?

focus.text: 16.b4 fixes the queenside. Black's b5- and c5-pawns are now permanent targets, and — this is the whole point — his rook, queen and knights get chained to defending them. That is weakness number one. But one weakness a good defender holds, so this is only half the plan: Karpov next tripled his major pieces on the a-file, traded the rooks off, and only THEN swung his knight and bishop toward the KINGSIDE, where the overstretched defense finally broke. Fix here, break there.

questions.prompt: You have a fixed weakness on one wing, but your opponent has just enough pieces to guard it and the position is static. What does the principle of two weaknesses prescribe?
options: Keep piling attackers onto the same weakness until sheer numbers break it.
Open a second front on the other wing, so the same defenders must cover two distant points at once.
Accept that one weakness is never enough and offer a draw.
questions.explain: Massing on a single point (option 1) fails against a defender who has enough guards for that one square — the attackers pile up but nothing gives. The win comes only from a SECOND, distant weakness: defensive pieces cannot be in two places, so shuttling pressure between the fronts eventually overloads them. Offering a draw (option 3) throws away a standard winning method.

questions.prompt: White has bound Black to the weak a5-pawn (weakness one), but Black's rook guards it and the queenside alone will not win. Playing for the win — make the move that begins weakness two.
questions.explain: Grabbing the a-pawn at once with Rc5 or Rxa5 trades into a level pawn ending Black holds — a single weakness the defender always covers. Winning that pawn is not the plan. Advancing a kingside pawn (g4/h4/f4, heading for g5/h5 or f5) manufactures a SECOND target near Black's king; only when his king and rook are stretched between both wings does the a-pawn actually fall.

questions.prompt: In the Karpov–Unzicker structure, White has fixed Black's queenside with a4, axb5, b4. Explain why that is only HALF of the winning plan, and what the second half is.
questions.modelAnswer: Fixing the queenside makes the first weakness and ties Black's pieces to defending b5/c5 — but a single weakness a good defender simply guards, and if White only keeps hammering the queenside the game stays blocked and drifts toward a draw. The second half is to create a SECOND weakness on the other wing (the kingside/centre) while Black is still chained to the first. With the defenders unable to cover both fronts, White shuttles his pieces between them until the overstretched defense drops material. The mistake to avoid is treating the fixed queenside as the whole plan — one weakness binds, it does not break; the win comes from opening the second front.
rubric: Identifies the fixed queenside as ONE weakness that binds Black's pieces to its defence.
States that a single weakness alone is holdable and does not win by itself.
Names creating a SECOND weakness on the other wing as the second half.
Explains the mechanism: the defenders cannot cover two distant fronts at once.
Avoids the error of just massing more force on the first weakness.

questions.prompt: Before you switch wings to open a second front, what must stay true of the FIRST weakness?
options: It must already have fallen — you cannot manage two weaknesses at once.
It must stay fixed and immobile, keeping the enemy pieces tied to it while you operate on the other wing.
Nothing — just attack wherever looks tempting; the first weakness takes care of itself.
questions.explain: If the first weakness is not fixed, the defender frees those pieces or gets counterplay the moment you leave — and the two-front stretch collapses. You do NOT need to win it first (option 1); grabbing it early usually just trades down and releases the bind. The fixed weakness must keep tying the defense down (option 2) while the second front does the breaking. Attacking at random (option 3) creates no bind and no stretch.

principle.markdown:
A locked position stays locked until a **pawn break** — a lever — opens a file or diagonal. The break is where closed games are won and lost, and the whole skill is one word: **timing**.

The rule is simple to say and hard to obey: **open the position only when it favours YOUR pieces, not your opponent's.** A break trades a closed structure for open lines, and open lines reward whoever is better developed and better placed to use them. So before you pull the lever, ask the prophylactic question — *who is ready?* If your rooks aren't on the file the break will open, if your worst piece is still at home, if the break just hands the opponent a passed pawn or a strong square — then it is **premature**, and the strong move is to keep it closed and keep improving. Petrosian's whole art is this restraint: prepare, improve, and refuse to release the tension one move before it helps you.

The other face of timing is the opposite instinct. When your pieces ARE ready — a lead in development, rooks aimed at a half-open file, the enemy king short of defenders — the break can be worth a **sacrifice**. Here the lever is not a quiet push but a calculated pawn or piece offer that rips the centre open before the defender can consolidate. This is Tal's and Fischer's territory: the position is objectively ripe, so you *calculate* the sac that blows it open rather than wait. Same question, opposite answer — because this time the readiness test comes back yes.

So the two instincts are not rivals; they are the same judgement. Keep-it-closed-and-improve and calculate-a-sac-and-blow-it-open are both answers to *who is ready to use the open lines?* Rushing a break before your pieces support it just creates weaknesses and loses the lever; refusing a break when everything is aimed and loaded wastes the position.
principle.remember: Open the position only when the open lines favour your pieces — prepare the break until they do, and when they do, don't flinch from a sacrifice to pull the lever.

So the question for White is not 'how do I break?' but 'who is ready?' — and the honest answer is nobody yet.

The locked d-pawns (d5 vs d6) fix the structure; the lever White is loading is e4-e5, the break that turns this wall of pawns into open lines against Black's king. Black has just played 9...Re8, eyeing the e-file. White is fully mobilised: knight on f3, bishop on e2, king about to be safe, the whole centre aimed forward. THIS is the readiness test coming back 'yes'. White to move.

ask.prompt: White to move. The pieces are developed and the centre is loaded. Pull the lever — play the break.
ask.explain: e5! is the thematic Benoni break, offered as a pawn: after 10...dxe5 11.fxe5 the f-file opens for the rook and the e5-pawn cramps Black, while d5-d6 looms as a passed pawn. Waiting is the mistake — a slow move like 10.Be3 or 10.Qc2 lets Black complete with ...Na6-c7 and ...b5, and the e5 lever never gets easier than it is right now with everything aimed at it. focus.text: 11.fxe5 rips the centre open. Compare this to the Ruy: there White refused to release the tension because nobody was ready; here White forces it open BECAUSE he is ready. Same judgement, opposite move — the pieces decided it.

16.d6 — the dividend. The break that opened the position also unleashed the passed d-pawn, wedged deep in Black's camp and splitting his position. The lever wasn't just about open lines; it was about what those lines and this pawn do once the structure cracks. That is what you calculate before you pull it.

questions.prompt: You have a locked centre and you are wondering whether to force it open with a pawn break. What is the single question that decides it?
options: Whichever side has more space should always break first.
Who is more ready to use the open lines the break will create?
Break whenever you can — an open position is always more winning than a closed one.
Never break a locked centre; keeping it closed is always safest.
questions.explain: Timing a break is one prophylactic question — who is ready to USE the lines it opens? Space (option 1) doesn't decide it; a break can hand your space advantage to a better-developed opponent. 'Always open' (option 3) is the impatient error that loses the lever by rushing it, and 'never open' (option 4) is the passive error that wastes a ripe position. Both Petrosian's restraint and Tal's sacrifice are the SAME answer to that one question — held or pulled depending on who is ready.

questions.prompt: King's Indian, locked centre (d5/e4 vs d6/e5). Black has spent moves preparing the kingside lever — rook to f7, knight to g6, ...h5 played, king tucked. It is finally time. Play the break.
questions.explain: ...g4! is the prepared lever: it opens the g- and h-files toward White's king exactly when Black's attackers are ready to pour in. The point of the exercise is that the SAME push a few moves earlier — before ...Rf7, ...Ng6 and ...h5 — would have been premature, met by fxg4 with nothing behind it. The break isn't strong because it's a break; it's strong because the pieces supporting it finally arrived. Rushing it is the classic mistake; here you've earned it.

questions.prompt: White (Benoni, big centre) has every piece developed and Black just played ...Re8. Why is this the moment to strike with 10.e5, even sacrificing the pawn?
options: Because a material sacrifice is always justified in a closed position.
Because White's pieces are fully mobilised and aimed at the centre, so opening lines now favours HIM before Black can consolidate.
Because White is losing and must complicate at any cost.
questions.explain: The sac is timed by readiness, not by desperation. e5 is right because White's development lead and piece placement mean the open lines will favour White the instant the centre cracks — the readiness test says yes. Sacrificing 'always' (option 1) ignores that a premature break with pieces at home just donates material, and complicating from a worse position (option 3) is a different, hope-based motive. Tal calculated these; he didn't gamble them.

questions.prompt: Closed Ruy Lopez: the centre is fully locked in tension (c5/d6/e5 vs d4/e4). In your own words, explain why White should NOT resolve the tension yet, and what he should do instead. What would a premature capture give away?
questions.modelAnswer: Nobody is ready to benefit from open lines yet, so resolving the tension only helps Black. 12.dxe5 dxe5 hands Black the open d-file and free, active development; 12.dxc5 dxc5 opens his game and, crucially, trades away the central tension — the lever White wants to keep loaded — for nothing. The correct plan is prophylactic restraint: keep the tension and improve the worst piece with 12.Nbd2, heading Nf1-g3, so that when White finally does break (a later d5 with tempo, or g4 on the wing) it happens on his terms. The mistake to avoid is treating 'I must do something with the centre' as a reason to release it — releasing tension before you're the one ready to use the open lines gives the opponent the very files and tempi you were sitting on.
rubric: Identifies that opening the centre now favours Black, not White.
Names a concrete drawback of a capture (open d-file / free tempo / lost tension), not just 'it's bad'.
Proposes keeping the tension and improving a piece (e.g. Nbd2-f1-g3) rather than any immediate break.
Frames the decision as 'who is ready to use the open lines?', not a fixed rule about capturing.
Avoids recommending a premature d5/dxe5/dxc5 before the pieces are routed.

principle.markdown:
In a fully locked position, the player who moves *for the sake of moving* usually loses. Every pawn advance fixes a target; every hasty piece sortie can be chased and cost a tempo. So the discipline of closed play is **patience**: improve your position by tiny, reversible increments — centralize the king, put each piece on its ideal square, keep every pawn where it cannot be attacked — and refuse to be the side that commits first.

This is not passivity. Waiting has a *purpose*: you are handing the obligation to move back to your opponent. When the structure is locked and useful moves run out, whoever must move first has to weaken something — advance a pawn, abandon a guarded square, misplace a piece. That is the zugzwang flavour of maneuvering: the **waiting move** is a weapon precisely because a good position plays itself while a cramped one runs out of good moves.

Karpov built a career on this — the "boa constrictor," tightening one coil at a time, never releasing the tension until the opponent had cracked; Carlsen grinds the same way, keeping a "nothing" position alive until the other side finally errs. The trap is impatience: forcing a break before your pieces are ready manufactures the first weakness *in your own camp*.

So: don't rush, don't weaken, improve to the maximum — then make **them** move.
principle.remember: Improve to the maximum without weakening, then hand the move back: in a locked position the side forced to commit first is the side that cracks.

focus.text: Look at the pawns: every file is blocked, all eight White pawns face a fixed Black pawn. There are no open lines, no targets, and the queens are off. A pawn break right now (c4 or f4) would only hand your opponent the first weakness. Before you force anything, ask the quiet question — which of your pieces is worst placed?

ask.prompt: White to move in a totally locked, queenless position. Resist the urge to break — improve your worst-placed piece instead. What is White's patient first move?
ask.explain: The break c4 (or f4) is the impatient mistake: it releases the tension, and after ...bxc4 bxc4 the b-file opens for Black's rooks against weaknesses you just created — you commit first, so you crack first. With no open files and no queens, the king is a fighting piece, and here it is your worst-placed one. Kf1 begins the march to d3, improving your position by a reversible increment while keeping every pawn intact — so Black, not you, is the side that eventually runs out of safe moves.

focus.text: Both kings march to the centre, but White is a tempo ahead and — crucially — has not touched a single pawn. Notice the mechanism: as long as White only improves, Black must either mirror (and stay a tempo behind) or run out of useful moves and weaken. Always having a quiet improving move in hand is the waiting move working as a weapon.

The king reaches d3: it shields e4 and c3 and stands ready to support a break once — and only once — the rest of the army is optimal. Compare the two roads from the diagram. The patient road improved a piece and kept the structure whole; the impatient c4 five moves ago would already have handed Black a target. Patience didn't draw the game — it built the winning position.

questions.prompt: You are the patient side in a fully locked position and you have run out of obviously useful moves. What is the point of a "waiting move" instead of forcing a pawn break?
options: To stall until the opponent offers a draw — closed positions are drawish anyway.
To hand the obligation to move back to the opponent, so they must be the one to advance a pawn or abandon a square — and weaken first.
To gain a tempo for a direct attack on the enemy king.
questions.explain: The stalling mindset (option 1) is exactly the trap this lesson kills — "nothing to do" is a feeling, not an assessment. A waiting move is not an attack either (option 3): there is no attack yet. Its purpose is zugzwang-flavoured — you keep a quiet improving move in reserve so that when useful moves run out, it is your opponent who must commit and weaken. Whoever moves first in a locked position cracks first.

questions.prompt: White to move — a fully locked, queenless position. You'd love to force matters with the break b4, but your pieces aren't ready. Improve your worst piece to its ideal square instead. Play the move.
questions.explain: b4 is the impatient error: after ...cxb4 cxb4 you have opened the c-file for Black's rook and left the d5- and b4-pawns as fresh targets — you committed first, so you weakened first. Instead Nc4 reroutes the knight to a protected outpost (defended by b3) that hits the backward d6-pawn and eyes b6; no Black pawn attacks it. Improve to the maximum first — the break can wait until your pieces have earned it.

questions.prompt: In the locked position from the illustration, Black simply mirrors your king march and you cannot make progress by force. In your own words: describe White's plan, explain concretely how a waiting move helps, and say what the impatient alternative would cost.
questions.modelAnswer: The plan is to improve to the maximum without touching the pawn structure: march the king to d3 (it defends e4 and c3 and will back a future break), place the rooks on the file a break will eventually open, and put every piece on its ideal square. Only when everything is optimal do you play a break (b4 or f4) — and you keep a quiet waiting move in reserve so that, if Black has mirrored you, you can pass the move back and force him to weaken (advance a pawn or leave a guarded square), creating the target you then attack. The impatient alternative is to break at once: an early c4 or f4 releases the tension while your own pieces are still passive, manufacturing the first weakness in your own camp and handing Black an open file. Patience here is not stalling — it is refusing to be the side that commits first.
rubric: Names a concrete improving target (e.g. king to d3, rooks to the file a break will open), not just "improve my position."
Explains the waiting move as passing the obligation to move to Black (the zugzwang idea), not as stalling for a draw.
Says the break is played only after the pieces are optimal — patience is preparation, not permanent passivity.
Identifies the cost of rushing: a premature break creates the first weakness in your own camp / opens a file for the opponent.

questions.prompt: Patience is the theme — but it is not the same as never acting. When does the disciplined closed-position player finally play the pawn break?
options: Never — in a locked position you keep waiting and steer for the draw.
Immediately, to seize the initiative before the opponent does.
Once the pieces are on their optimal squares and the break opens a line toward a concrete target — patience is preparation, then you strike.
questions.explain: Option 1 is passivity — the failure mode that masquerades as patience; a waiting move is a means to force the opponent to crack, not a way to shuffle toward a draw. Option 2 is the impatience the whole lesson warns against: breaking before your pieces are ready creates weaknesses in your own camp. The break is right only when it is fully prepared and opens lines toward a real weakness (option 3) — you wait in order to strike harder, not instead of striking.

principle.markdown:
**Space** is simply room: more squares for your pieces to work, fewer for the opponent's. But space is a wasting asset — it only counts while the opponent stays cramped. Convert it, or it evaporates.

Two disciplines turn a space edge into a win. First, **keep pieces on the board.** The cramped side is desperate to trade, because every exchange gives their remaining pieces the room they lack. So you do the opposite of the attacker's instinct: you *avoid* swaps and keep the board full, so their army stays stepped on its own toes.

Second, **restriction** — take away the opponent's active moves and freeing pawn breaks one at a time, until all that is left to them is shuffling. This is Karpov's "boa constrictor": grab space, deny every break, occupy the one open file and the key holes, and only *then* open a second front. The opponent suffocates before you ever have to calculate a thing. Counterplay you prevented is worth more than an attack you have to defend.

The trap is impatience. A space advantage tempts you to cash it in with a break or a trade — and both hand the cramped side exactly the air they were gasping for.
principle.remember: Convert space by keeping pieces on and denying every freeing break — squeeze the counterplay to zero, then open a second front.

Black has just replayed his knight to c6 to hit the d4-pawn and pry the centre open — the cramped side's whole hope is to trade and breathe. White must decide the fate of the centre. Do you keep the tension, or resolve it?

ask.prompt: White to move. Black wants the centre opened so his pieces get air. What claims maximum space and slams the door instead?
ask.explain: Holding the tension with a move like Be3 or trading with dxe5 is exactly what Black wants — dxe5 dxe5 frees his game and invites the swaps that relieve a cramp. d5 does the opposite: it grabs the whole centre, locks the position, and kicks the c6-knight into a three-move retreat (Nd8–b7). Space first; open the position only when it suits YOU.

focus.text: 13. d5 gains a permanent central space edge and freezes the pawns (d5/e4 against d6/e5). The c6-knight is shoved back to d8 and must spend three tempi rerouting — White is effectively a piece up in the sector that matters while Black untangles.

16. b4 claims the queenside too. After the a-file was opened by axb5 axb5, White owns the only open file and now stakes out space on both wings. In the game Black soon locked with ...c4, surrendering his last break: from there Karpov simply improved every piece (the famous Ba7 clamp, doubling rooks on the a-file) while Unzicker had no active move at all, and was slowly strangled. Space, then total restriction — the counterplay reached zero before a single line was forced open.

questions.prompt: You have a clear space advantage in a closed position. What general rule follows?
options: Trade as many pieces as possible to convert space into a simpler, winning position.
Keep pieces on and deny the cramped side any freeing break; avoid trades that give their pieces room.
Sacrifice a pawn immediately to rip the position open before the opponent consolidates.
questions.explain: Trading (option 1) is precisely what the cramped defender is praying for — every exchange hands their stepped-on pieces the room they lacked, and your space edge dissolves. Sacrificing to open lines (option 3) throws the bind away for a speculative attack. With more space you keep the board full and squeeze; the exchange rule flips when you're the one with space.

questions.prompt: White to move. Black has a permanent hole on d5 and a bad light-squared bishop biting on his own pawns. Play the move that plants a piece where Black can never chase it and restricts his whole position.
questions.explain: A routine developing move like Re1 or Qc2 lets Black untangle with ...d5 or ...Nd7 and free himself — the mistake is treating a static edge as if it will keep. Nd5 seizes the hole permanently: the outpost hits e7 and f6 and dominates the b7-bishop and f6-knight at once. Even if Black trades it (...Nxd5 exd5), the recapture leaves White a protected passed pawn and still more space — the clamp only tightens.

questions.prompt: In Karpov–Unzicker, after White clamped the centre with d5 and the queenside with a4/b4, Black played ...c4. Why did this suit White?
options: It opened the c-file and gave Black's rooks active counterplay.
It froze the pawn chains and gave up Black's last pawn break, leaving him only shuffling moves while White maneuvered freely.
It won the b4-pawn by force and equalized on the spot.
questions.explain: ...c4 releases the central tension but at a fatal price: with every pawn now fixed, Black has no break left and no active plan — he can only wait. Reading ...c4 as 'activity on the c-file' (option 1) is the error: the file stays jammed shut by the c4/b4 pawns. It is a concession that completes White's restriction, after which Karpov improved his pieces at leisure and Black suffocated.

questions.prompt: This is the Karpov–Unzicker position after 16. b4, White to think about the coming plan. In your own words: how should White (with more space) convert this, and what is the mistake that would throw the advantage away?
questions.modelAnswer: Don't hurry and don't trade. With more space White keeps pieces on so Black's stay cramped, and takes the only open file (the a-file) with the rooks. Then improve every piece to its best square behind the lines — a knight toward c4/d5-type holes, the light bishop rerouted, the dark bishop swinging to a7 to clamp — and provoke Black into fixing his structure (...c4), which kills his last break. Only once Black is completely restricted and has no counter-break do you open a second front on the kingside. The mistake is impatience: forcing a break early or swapping pieces to 'simplify' hands the cramped defender exactly the air he needs — each trade gives his pieces room and each premature break gives him lines, dissolving the space advantage you spent moves building. Suffocate the counterplay first; open the position last.
rubric: Says keep pieces on / avoid trades because the cramped side wants exchanges.
Names seizing the open a-file and/or occupying a key hole or outpost.
Includes provoking a second weakness / opening a second front only after Black is restricted.
Names the mistake: rushing a break or trading pieces early frees the cramped defender and dissolves the space edge.
